summary.text:
Two applications of the Pfaff–Saalschütz identity and a rearrangement of the resulting double sum give
\[(3n+1)a(n)=(n+1)\sum_{2j\le n+1}\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\binom{2n-j}{n}^{2}\binom{n+j}{j}.\]
For every summand, the range assumptions force \(p\mid\binom{2n-j}{n}\), supplying \(p^2\), while the third factor of \(p\) comes from \(\binom{n+j}{j}\) if \(n+j\ge p\), from \(n+1\) if \(n+1=p\), and otherwise from \(\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\) by reduction modulo \(p\); since \(3n+1\) lies strictly between \(2p\) and \(3p\), it is coprime to \(p\), so it can be cancelled.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n \binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}\binom{3n+2k}{n}.
\]
We prove that if \(p\ge 5\) is prime and
\[
\left\lceil\frac{2p+1}{3}\right\rceil\le n\le p-1,
\]
then \(p^3\mid a(n)\).

The proof has two parts. First we derive a binomial identity that rewrites \((3n+1)a(n)\) as a sum whose terms visibly contain two factors of \(p\). Then we show, by a case split, that every term contains a third factor of \(p\).

## 1. A Pfaff–Saalschütz identity

For a rational number \(x\) and a nonnegative integer \(r\), write
\[
(x)_r=x(x+1)\cdots(x+r-1),\qquad (x)_0=1
\]
for the rising factorial. We will use the following division-free form of the Pfaff–Saalschütz summation:
\[
\sum_{s=0}^{k}\binom{k}{s}(A)_s(B)_s(C+s)_{k-s}(C-A-B)_{k-s}
=(C-A)_k(C-B)_k. \tag{1}
\]

For completeness, this identity follows by a direct telescoping induction. Define
\[
F_{k,s}=\binom{k}{s}(A)_s(B)_s(C+s)_{k-s}(C-A-B)_{k-s}
\]
and
\[
G_{k,s}=\binom{k}{s}(A)_{s+1}(B)_{s+1}(C+s)_{k-s}(C-A-B)_{k-s}.
\]
Using \((x)_{r+1}=(x)_r(x+r)\), Pascal's identity, and
\[
\binom{k}{s+1}(s+1)=\binom{k}{s}(k-s),
\]
one obtains
\[
F_{k+1,0}=(C-A+k)(C-B+k)F_{k,0}-G_{k,0},
\]
and, for \(0\le s\le k\),
\[
F_{k+1,s+1}=(C-A+k)(C-B+k)F_{k,s+1}+G_{k,s}-G_{k,s+1}.
\]
Here terms with a lower binomial index exceeding the upper one are zero. Summing these equations over \(s\), the \(G\)-terms telescope, and the shifted \(F\)-sum differs from the unshifted one exactly by the boundary term already appearing in the first equation. Thus, if \(S_k=\sum_{s=0}^k F_{k,s}\), then
\[
S_{k+1}=(C-A+k)(C-B+k)S_k.
\]
Since \(S_0=1\), induction gives
\[
S_k=(C-A)_k(C-B)_k,
\]
which is (1).

We also use the elementary duplication formula
\[
(x)_{2r}=4^r\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)_r
                 \left(\frac{x+1}{2}\right)_r, \tag{2}
\]
obtained by separating the even and odd factors in the product defining \((x)_{2r}\).

## 2. The transformation of \(a(n)\)

Apply (1) with
\[
A=-\frac n2,\qquad B=-\frac{n+1}{2},\qquad C=n+\frac12.
\]
Using (2) on the two products occurring on each side gives
\[
(3n+1)_{2k}
=
\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j} (-(n+1))_{2j}
\frac{(2n+2j+1)_{2(k-j)}(2n+1)_{k-j}}
     {(n+j+1)_{k-j}}. \tag{3}
\]
All denominators here are nonzero, because their initial values are positive integers.

We now convert rising factorials into ordinary factorials, using
\[
(r+1)_s=\frac{(r+s)!}{r!},
\qquad
(-r)_s=(-1)^s\frac{r!}{(r-s)!}\quad(s\le r), \tag{4}
\]
with \((-r)_s=0\) when \(s>r\). Substitution of (3) into the factorial expression for the original summand yields
\[
\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}\binom{3n+2k}{n}
   =\sum_{j=0}^k f(n,k,j), \tag{5}
\]
where, as a rational expression,
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(n,k,j)={}&\binom nk^2\binom kj (-(n+1))_{2j}\,(3n)!\,(2n+k-j)!\,(n+j)!\\
&\big/\left((2n+2j)!\,(2n)!\,(n!)^2\,k!\right).
\end{aligned} \tag{6}
\]
To see (5) directly, write
\[
\binom{3n+2k}{n}=\frac{(3n+2k)!}{n!(2n+2k)!},
\qquad
\binom{n+k}{k}=\frac{(n+k)!}{k!n!},
\]
replace \((3n+2k)!/(3n)!\) by the left side of (3), and use
\[
(2n+2j+1)_{2(k-j)}= rac{(2n+2k)!}{(2n+2j)!},
\]
\[
(2n+1)_{k-j}=\frac{(2n+k-j)!}{(2n)!},
\qquad
(n+j+1)_{k-j}=\frac{(n+k)!}{(n+j)!}.
\]
After cancellation, the resulting summand is precisely (6).

We sum (5) over \(0\le k\le n\) and interchange the order of summation:
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^n\sum_{k=j}^n f(n,k,j). \tag{7}
\]
It remains to evaluate the inner sum. Put
\[
N=n-j,\qquad k=j+m,
\]
so that \(0\le m\le N\). A second application of (1), now with
\[
A=-N,\qquad B=2(j+N)+1,
\qquad C=j+1,
\]
gives, after conversion by (4),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{m=0}^{N}
 \binom{j+N}{j+m}\binom Nm
 \frac{(2(j+N)+m)!}{(j+m)!}\\
&\hspace{2cm}=
\frac{(2(j+N))!\,(j+2N)!^2}
{N!\,(j+N)!^3}. \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here is how (8) follows from (1). For the stated parameters, the right side of (1) is
\[
(j+N+1)_N\,(-(j+2N))_N
=(-1)^N\frac{(j+2N)!^2}{(j+N)!^2}.
\]
In the summand on the left, \((-N)_m=(-1)^mN!/(N-m)!\), while the remaining negative rising factorial is
\[
(-(j+N))_{N-m}
=(-1)^{N-m}\frac{(j+N)!}{(j+m)!}.
\]
The signs combine to \((-1)^N\). Expressing the other rising factorial as
\[
(2(j+N)+1)_m= rac{(2(j+N)+m)!}{(2(j+N))!}
\]
and converting the ordinary binomial coefficients to factorials gives (8) after cancelling the common factor \((-1)^N\).

Inserting (6) into the inner sum in (7), using
\[
\binom{j+N}{j+m}\binom{j+m}{j}
= inom{j+N}{j}\binom Nm,
\]
and then applying (8), evaluates that inner sum. The remaining factorials simplify as follows. If \(2j>n+1\), then
\[
(-(n+1))_{2j}=0,
\]
so the inner sum vanishes. If \(2j\le n+1\), then
\[
(-(n+1))_{2j}= rac{(n+1)!}{(n+1-2j)!},
\]
because \(2j\) is even. Converting all remaining factorial ratios to binomial coefficients gives
\[
\sum_{k=j}^n f(n,k,j)
= rac{n+1}{3n+1}
 \binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}
 \binom{2n-j}{n}^{2}
 \binom{n+j}{j}. \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, in (8), with \(N=n-j\), one has
\[
j+2N=2n-j,
\]
and the factorials pair respectively into
\[
\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j},\qquad
\binom{2n-j}{n}^2,
\qquad
\binom{n+j}{j};
\]
the uncancelled consecutive-factor ratio is exactly \((n+1)/(3n+1)\).

Combining (7) and (9), and clearing the denominator, proves the key identity
\[
\boxed{
(3n+1)a(n)
=(n+1)\sum_{\substack{0\le j\le n\\2j\le n+1}}
 \binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}
 \binom{2n-j}{n}^{2}
 \binom{n+j}{j}.
} \tag{10}
\]
Although derived as an identity of rational numbers, both sides of (10) are integers, so (10) is an ordinary integer identity.

## 3. A basic binomial divisibility fact

We use the following standard consequence of Legendre's formula (equivalently, of the one-carry case of Kummer's theorem): if \(p\) is prime, \(0\le r,s<p\), and \(r+s\ge p\), then
\[
p\mid \binom{r+s}{r}. \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, \((r+s)!\) contains one factor of \(p\), whereas neither \(r!\) nor \(s!\) contains a factor of \(p\).

We also use the following special case of Lucas's theorem. If
\[
M=qp+r_0,\qquad 0\le r_0<p,
\]
and \(0\le t<p\), then
\[
\binom Mt\equiv \binom{r_0}{t}\pmod p. \tag{12}
\]
In particular, if \(r_0<t<p\), then \(p\mid\binom Mt\).

## 4. Divisibility of every term in (10)

Assume now that \(p\ge5\) is prime and
\[
\left\lceil\frac{2p+1}{3}\right\rceil\le n\le p-1.
\]
The lower bound is equivalent to
\[
2p+1\le 3n. \tag{13}
\]
Fix an index \(j\) occurring in (10), so
\[
0\le j\le n,
\qquad 2j\le n+1. \tag{14}
\]
Denote the corresponding summand, including the outside factor \(n+1\), by
\[
T_j=(n+1)
 \binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}
 \binom{2n-j}{n}^{2}
 \binom{n+j}{j}. \tag{15}
\]
We prove \(p^3\mid T_j\).

First, \(p\mid\binom{2n-j}{n}\). Write
\[
\binom{2n-j}{n}=\binom{n+(n-j)}{n}.
\]
Both \(n\) and \(n-j\) are less than \(p\), since \(n\le p-1\). Moreover, (13) and (14) imply
\[
2(2n-j)=4n-2j\ge 4n-(n+1)=3n-1\ge2p,
\]
so \(2n-j\ge p\). Thus (11), with \(r=n\) and \(s=n-j\), gives
\[
p\mid\binom{2n-j}{n}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
p^2\mid\binom{2n-j}{n}^2. \tag{16}
\]
It remains to find one further factor of \(p\) in
\[
(n+1)\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\binom{n+j}{j}. \tag{17}
\]
We split into cases.

### Case 1: \(p\le n+j\)

Since both \(n<p\) and \(j<p\), (11), applied to \(n+j\), gives
\[
p\mid\binom{n+j}{j}. \tag{18}
\]
Together with (16), this proves \(p^3\mid T_j\).

### Case 2: \(n+j<p\)

If \(n+1=p\), then the factor \(n+1\) in (17) itself supplies the third factor of \(p\), and again \(p^3\mid T_j\).

It remains to consider the subcase
\[
n+1<p. \tag{19}
\]
Set
\[
t=n+1-2j.
\]
By (14), \(t\ge0\); and by (19), \(t<p\). From (13) and (19),
\[
2p<3n+1<3p.
\]
Thus
\[
3n+1=2p+r_0,
\qquad r_0=3n+1-2p,
\qquad 0\le r_0<p. \tag{20}
\]
The assumption \(n+j<p\) implies
\[
2n+2j<2p,
\]
and hence
\[
r_0=3n+1-2p<n+1-2j=t. \tag{21}
\]
Applying (12) to (20) and using (21), we obtain
\[
\binom{3n+1}{t}
\equiv \binom{r_0}{t}=0\pmod p.
\]
Therefore
\[
p\mid\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}. \tag{22}
\]
This supplies the third factor of \(p\), so (16) and (22) give \(p^3\mid T_j\).

We have proved in every case that every summand \(T_j\) on the right side of (10) is divisible by \(p^3\). Hence
\[
p^3\mid (3n+1)a(n). \tag{23}
\]

## 5. Cancellation of \(3n+1\)

It remains to show that \(p\nmid 3n+1\). Suppose to the contrary that
\[
3n+1=cp
\]
for an integer \(c\). From (13),
\[
3n+1\ge2p+2,
\]
so \(c>2\). On the other hand, \(n\le p-1\) gives
\[
3n+1\le3p-2<3p,
\]
so \(c<3\). No integer \(c\) satisfies \(2<c<3\), a contradiction. Thus
\[
\gcd(p,3n+1)=1,
\]
and therefore also
\[
\gcd(p^3,3n+1)=1.
\]
Euclid's lemma applied to (23) now allows cancellation of the factor \(3n+1\), yielding
\[
p^3\mid a(n).
\]
This proves the conjecture for every prime \(p\ge5\) and every integer \(n\) in the stated interval.
